approach.expect: No maintained trail leads directly to Mount Barnes — it is a cross-country side-trip off the Bailey Range Traverse. Two main approaches: (1) West via Sol Duc Trailhead — Sol Duc River Trail up to Bogachiel Peak/High Divide (filling water at Heart Lake, the last reliable source for miles), then off-trail east along the Bailey Range crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin, and Stephen Peak to Bear Pass — roughly 3-5 days of travel before reaching Barnes. (2) East via the Elwha River Trail — historically from Whiskey Bend Trailhead (about 26 mi one way with ~6,100 ft gain to the trail's end near Elwha Basin/Dodwell-Rixon Pass); as of the September 2024 Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, Whiskey Bend is closed to vehicles, adding an extra 6.2 mi one-way walk or bike from the Madison Falls parking area just to reach the trailhead. From a camp near Bear Pass or a nearby meadow, the final summit push contours scree and lingering snow patches southeast, then curls north on a boot track up a moderate scree slope to the Class 2 summit — a few hours round trip once camp is established.

approach.expect: Getting to the trailhead is currently part of the approach: a 2023-24 washout closed Olympic Hot Springs Road to vehicles at the Madison Falls parking area, and as of the NPS's 2024-2025 advisories that closure adds roughly 7 miles each way of road walking or biking just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road remains open to foot/bike traffic beyond Madison Falls). From Whiskey Bend, the actual hike-in follows the Elwha River Trail, a well-graded historic path along the river's east bank that passes the old Geyser Valley homestead sites (Michael's Cabin, Humes Ranch) in the first mile or two. The trail is mellow by Olympic standards, staying under roughly 2,000 ft of gain through its first 15+ miles, and passes Lillian River junction (~4 mi), Mary's Falls Camp (8.8 mi), Canyon Camp, Elkhorn Guard Station, and Stony Point as it winds upstream through old-growth forest with the Elwha River itself as a constant, reliable water source. Camp Wilder and Hayes River Guard Station mark roughly the trail's halfway point. Continue south to Elwha Basin and Chicago Camp (roughly 24-26 trail miles from Whiskey Bend), where the Elwha River must be forded — NPS explicitly flags this crossing as one to check conditions on beforehand, since it can be genuinely hazardous in early-season high water or after rain. At and beyond Chicago Camp the maintained trail effectively dissolves into the Elwha Basin, and travel becomes cross-country: a boot-beaten climbers' path continues up the valley headwaters toward the obvious white tongue of the Elwha Snow Finger, a permanent, avalanche-fed snowfield filling the bedrock gully that leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass (4,763'). The Snow Finger is the standard way through this section — carry an ice axe and know self-arrest. Recent parties note the snowpack has been thinning in late summer, exposing an opening moat, running water under the snow, and rockfall funneling off the surrounding walls, so climb it early in the day and reassess if it looks broken up; NPS notes snow can linger above Chicago Camp into July. From the top of the Snow Finger at Dodwell-Rixon Pass, Mount Dana sits several miles east-northeast (its coordinates place it roughly 5 miles from the pass, closer to the Mount Norton/Elwha-headwaters side of the range than to the main Carrie-Ferry-Pulitzer crest). There is no path here; parties pick a line across talus, heather benches, and lingering snow patches toward Dana's western slopes for the final class 2 scramble to the 6,214' summit. Water becomes scarce above the pass, so carry enough for a high camp. Given the roughly 70-mile round-trip distance, this is realistically a multi-day trip (3+ days) with a high camp near Dodwell-Rixon Pass or in the upper Elwha basin, not a car-to-car push, and solid off-trail navigation skill is essential once you're past Chicago Camp.

approach.expect: Mount Wilder sits deep in the Elwha drainage and this is a genuine multi-day backpack approach, not a day hike-in. From the Whiskey Bend trailhead (currently reached by an extra ~7-mile road-walk/bike-in from the washout near Madison Falls on Olympic Hot Springs Road, per NPS), follow the Elwha River Trail south along the river's east bank through old-growth lowland forest. Established waypoints/camps along the way (mileages approximate, gathered from NPS and trip-report cross-referencing): the Humes Ranch cutoff around 2.7 mi, Lillian River Camp around 4.9 mi (reliable water, log crossing of the Lillian River), Mary's Falls around 6.9 mi, Canyon Camp around 9.6 mi (trail narrows through a rocky gorge section), Elkhorn around 11.4 mi (old guard-station clearing, bear wire), and Hayes River Guard Station around 12 mi (junction with the Hayes River/Dodger Point trail). Continue upriver to Camp Wilder, roughly 16-17 miles from Whiskey Bend (established campsites, bear wire, small shelter), which sits in the river bottom directly below the peak's steep south face and is the logical base camp for the climb. Water is abundant along the river trail (numerous tributary crossings) but there is no bridge maintenance guarantee on side creeks — expect to rock-hop or ford minor tributaries, higher and faster in early season. From Camp Wilder there is no maintained trail to the summit: leave the river trail and climb north/northeast off-trail, first through streamside brush and old forest, then heather benches and talus, to gain the peak's south ridge. The south aspect of Mount Wilder rises nearly 3,800 feet in under two miles, so expect sustained, steep, trail-less travel on a mix of open slope, talus, and brush, with real route-finding needed to link the cleanest line to the ridge crest — there is no cairned or established scramble path, and this peak has no recorded first ascent date, reflecting how rarely it's visited. Top off water at Camp Wilder or a tributary before starting the climb, since it is scarce higher on the ridge.
approach.value: Mount Wilder sits deep in the Elwha drainage and this is a genuine multi-day backpack approach, not a day hike-in. From the Whiskey Bend trailhead (reached by an extra ~7-mile road-walk/bike-in from Madison Falls, where Olympic Hot Springs Road has been closed to vehicles since November 2017 flood damage), follow the Elwha River Trail south along the river's east bank through old-growth lowland forest. Established waypoints/camps along the way (mileages approximate, gathered from NPS and trip-report cross-referencing): the Humes Ranch cutoff around 2.7 mi, Lillian River Camp around 4.9 mi (reliable water, log crossing of the Lillian River), Mary's Falls around 6.9 mi, Canyon Camp around 9.6 mi (trail narrows through a rocky gorge section), Elkhorn around 11.4 mi (old guard-station clearing, bear wire), and Hayes River Guard Station around 12 mi (junction with the Hayes River/Dodger Point trail). Continue upriver to Camp Wilder, roughly 16-17 miles from Whiskey Bend (established campsites, bear wire, small shelter), which sits in the river bottom directly below the peak's steep south face and is the logical base camp for the climb. Water is abundant along the river trail (numerous tributary crossings) but there is no bridge maintenance guarantee on side creeks — expect to rock-hop or ford minor tributaries, higher and faster in early season. From Camp Wilder there is no maintained trail to the summit: leave the river trail and climb north/northeast off-trail, first through streamside brush and old forest, then heather benches and talus, to gain the peak's south ridge. The south aspect of Mount Wilder rises nearly 3,800 feet in under two miles, so expect sustained, steep, trail-less travel on a mix of open slope, talus, and brush, with real route-finding needed to link the cleanest line to the ridge crest — there is no cairned or established scramble path, and this peak has no recorded first ascent date, reflecting how rarely it's visited. Top off water at Camp Wilder or a tributary before starting the climb, since it is scarce higher on the ridge.

approach.expect: Two realistic approach corridors exist, both multi-day: (1) North Fork Quinault side — from the North Fork Quinault Trailhead at the end of the North Shore Road (not the South Shore Road, which leads to Graves Creek and the East Fork instead), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail or the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail (via Three Lakes and Kimta Peak) to Low Divide, roughly 16-20 miles one-way depending on the line chosen, then cross-country/climbers'-path to Seattle Meadows below the peak's south side. (2) Elwha side — from the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road to it has been closed to vehicles at Madison Falls since a 2021 washout, adding about seven miles each way on foot or bike), follow the Elwha River Trail up the Elwha valley toward Elwha Basin/Low Divide (on the order of 20+ miles one-way), then leave trail to climb into Seattle Creek Basin or Noyes Basin on the peak's northeast side. Either way, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp, with several thousand feet of trail gain before any scrambling begins. The Seattle Creek Basin approach (Elwha side) follows the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, forcing a steep, brushy bushwhack up onto the Mt. Noyes-Mt. Seattle ridge — expect slow going in heavy brush low down.

approach.expect: With the historic Staircase (North Fork Skokomish) approach currently closed, the practical way in is now from the Duckabush Trailhead via Duckabush Trail #803. The tread starts easy for about 2.4 miles to Little Hump, then climbs the steep, loose-rock switchbacks of Big Hump before mellowing again to the Olympic National Park boundary around mile 6.2-6.7. Continue up the valley past 5 Mile Camp (a popular fishing/camping flat by the river) and 10 Mile Camp (~mile 12), where the trail's grade eases through old-growth forest along the Duckabush River — reliable water the whole way, though treat it. Beyond 10 Mile Camp the trail steepens again through the rougher upper-valley tread toward the Duckabush Camp junction with the O'Neil Pass/North Fork Skokomish Trail; from there it's a tough, sustained climb — the last mile notably steep — up to Marmot Lake (roughly 20-21 miles from the trailhead), a good base camp near Hart Lake (0.9 mi), Lake LaCrosse (1.4 mi), and O'Neil Pass (1.2 mi). From Marmot Lake, drop back to the Home Sweet Home junction and climb the connector trail over First Divide (4,688 ft) — the old link to the closed Staircase side — then leave maintained trail to angle cross-country/climber's-path up open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Given the mileage (~29 miles one-way), most parties treat this as a multi-day trip with a camp at Marmot Lake or Home Sweet Home rather than a car-to-car push.

approach.expect: From US-101 at Brinnon, turn onto Dosewallips Road and drive roughly 8.5 miles to the road-end parking — the road beyond has been closed to vehicles since a 2002 flood and remains closed indefinitely as of recent seasons; park here (a mountain bike is a real time-saver for the road-walk ahead). Walk about a mile up the closed road and follow the bypass trail around the washout — a short ~0.3-mile detour with a few switchbacks past old-growth trees — then rejoin the abandoned roadbed and continue roughly 5.6 more miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station (1,600 ft). From the ranger station, pick up the Dosewallips River Trail for 1.4 miles to its junction with the West Fork Dosewallips Trail (Trail #1010); bear onto the West Fork Trail and follow the river upstream past a string of established camps — Dose Forks, Big Timber, Diamond Meadows — to Honeymoon Meadows (3,527 ft, about 8 trail-miles from the ranger station). Expect at least one calf-to-knee-deep ford of the West Fork in this stretch depending on season and snowmelt. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia toward Anderson Pass (4,464 ft), the low divide between the Quinault and Dosewallips drainages. Leave the maintained trail here and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a high camp on a snowy saddle above a small tarn (Anderson/Valkyrie Lake, ~5,100 ft) — most parties budget 7-9 hours trailhead-to-camp. From high camp, traverse above the tarn (often still frozen) and climb the steep snow finger leading up to Flypaper Pass (~6,500 ft); glacier recession has steepened this finger considerably beyond older published descriptions, with the crux section now estimated at 40+ degrees late in the season — plan to be through it before it melts out (ideally spring/early summer) and expect firm or icy snow requiring an ice axe and crampons. Water is reliable along the West Fork the entire way in and again at the tarn near high camp; carry what you need above that.
